title: Diet Drinks or Water? A Two-Year Weight Study
paragraphs: Diet soft drinks occupy an awkward place in nutrition advice: they help people cut sugar, but they are often suspected of stimulating appetite and quietly sabotaging weight loss. A two-year randomised trial from the universities of Liverpool and Leeds, published in the British Journal of Nutrition, suggests those fears may be overstated.

In the SWITCH trial, 493 adults with overweight or obesity were assigned at random to drink either water or diet beverages containing aspartame, acesulfame-K or sucralose, within a structured behavioural weight-management programme. The final year was designed to test whether participants could sustain their results once that support had been withdrawn.

Among those who completed the study, the diet drink group had lost 4.8 kilograms and the water group 3.7 kilograms, a gap that was not statistically significant and which the authors interpret as evidence of equivalence. Caution is warranted, though: the research was funded by the American Beverage Association, albeit with the investigators retaining control of the analysis, it was conducted at a single site and it suffered considerable dropout. The findings also sit uneasily with World Health Organization guidance, which advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.

questions.q: Why do the authors speak of “equivalence” rather than an advantage for diet drinks?
questions.a: Because the difference between the groups was not statistically significant.

questions.q: What was the purpose of the final year without support?
questions.a: To test whether participants could maintain their weight loss on their own.

questions.q: How do the findings relate to WHO guidance?
questions.a: They appear to conflict with the WHO’s advice not to rely on non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.
